query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized via rapid heating and cooling, a controlled, short dwell time at the peak temperature permits sufficient atomic interdiffusion to homogenize the precursor mixture and favor single-phase nucleation. In contrast, insufficient diffusion time during ultrafast heating locks in compositional inhomogeneities that lead to phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A precursor mixture containing more than five noble metal components with an initially heterogeneous spatial distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled dwell time at the peak temperature during synthesis, thereby deliberately extending the time available for atomic diffusion prior to cooling.
generation.conditions: Rapid heating and cooling conditions are maintained while varying the peak-temperature dwell time. The composition remains fixed (noble metal–based high-entropy alloy with >5 elements), and the nanoparticles are synthesized under kinetic regimes where diffusion and nucleation compete.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic interdiffusion (and resulting local elemental homogeneity) prior to nucleation serves as the mediator between synthesis conditions and the resulting crystal structure.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, increased atomic mobility allows for enhanced interdiffusion; a brief imposed dwell time enables the constituent noble metals to achieve sufficient mixing. This uniformity facilitates the nucleation of a single-phase solid-solution. Without this controlled hold, local inhomogeneities become ‘frozen in’ by rapid cooling, leading to phase separation, segregation, and irregular particle morphologies.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with an optimally extended dwell time will exhibit more uniform, single-phase solid-solution structures with fewer signs of elemental segregation, compared to baseline particles synthesized under standard rapid heating/cooling conditions with negligible dwell time.
generation.baseline: Synthesis under rapid heating and cooling with little or no dwell time at peak temperature, leading to observable phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (more than five elements) synthesized under rapid transient conditions. It may not hold if dwell times are so long that conventional diffusion or coarsening dominates, or if the synthesis temperature deviates significantly from that required for effective atomic mobility without triggering decomposition.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dwell time and specific temperature window for achieving the desired atomic homogeneity are not precisely known and may vary with the specific noble metal composition and particle size.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under identical rapid heating and cooling conditions while systematically varying the dwell time at the peak temperature (e.g., no dwell, intermediate dwell, extended dwell). Use structural characterization (XRD, electron microscopy) and elemental mapping (EDS) to assess phase purity and homogeneity.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to determine phase composition
High-resolution electron microscopy to examine particle morphology
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess elemental distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the dwell time does not lead to a systematic improvement in the appearance of a uniform single-phase structure (or if an extended dwell time unexpectedly increases phase separation and elemental segregation compared to the baseline), then the mechanistic hypothesis would be falsified.

High Entropy Oxide Phases with Perovskite Structure

Abstract: AbstractThe possibility of the formation of high entropy single-phase perovskites using solid-state sintering was investigated. The BaO–SrO–CaO–MgO–PbO–TiO2, BaO–SrO–CaO–MgO–PbO–Fe2O3 and Na2O–K2O–CaO–La2O3–Ce2O3–TiO2 oxide systems were investigated. The optimal synthesis temperature is found between 1150 and 1400 °C, at which the microcrystalline single phase with perovskite structure was produced. The morphology, chemical composition, crystal parameters and dielectric properties were studied and compared with that of pure BaTiO3. According to the EDX data, the single-phase product has a formula of Na0.30K0.07Ca0.24La0.18Ce0.21TiO3 and a cubic structure.Keywords: phase equilibria, multicomponent oxides, high entropy phases, perovskite, solid-phase sintering

Conclusions: A high entropy single-phase product with a perovskite structure was obtained in the present work. The calculated formula of the substituted phase was Na0.30K0.07Ca0.24La0.18Ce0.21TiO3.
